Encik Mohd Zabidi Md Nor’s Media Interview on Islamic Finance
Speaker
: Mohd Zabidi bin Md Noor
Venue
:
Delivery Date
:
29 Jun. 2016
A. BIG PICTURE
1. What are the major wins for Islamic finance since its first introduction to the nation?
The Islamic finance in Malaysia has made significant achievements over the past three decades. I would like to highlight three milestones which clearly encapsulate the phases of developments that the industry has gone through since its inception:
The first is the transformation of Islamic finance in Malaysia from a niche market into the mainstream that has enabled Islamic finance to offer competitive financial solutions.
This transformation is supported by strong foundations resulting from synergistic infrastructural developments, continuous institutional building, and robust regulatory and supervisory framework that have been put in place for over three decades. The market has grown by leaps and bounds. Prior to 2000, there were only two Islamic banks and two takaful operators in the country with total market share and takaful penetration rate of less than 5%. Now, Islamic banking assets have grown to capture more than a quarter (27%) of the total banking system while the takaful sector has increased its penetration rate to 14.8% of the populations. BNM has published our comprehensive statistical database that captures the growth of Islamic banking and takaful, alongside their conventional counterparts to allow continuous progress of the industry’s growth and achievements. The key statistics have been published for many years in our Financial Stability and Payment Systems Report, while extensive data can be found in the Bank’s Monthly Statistical Bulletin that is available in the Bank’s portal. In terms of market players, there are now 16 Islamic banks and 11 takaful operators that offer competitive financial solutions with more than 100 financial products that are beyond the basic financial services to also include wealth management products, corporate financial solutions and investment banking services. Financial inclusion has also been strengthened over the years with Islamic financing to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) showing an encouraging upward trend of 29% average annual growth rate for the period 2010-2015. Financing opportunities for entrepreneurs are expected to be further enhanced with the recently launched Investment Account Platform (IAP) that serves as an online marketplace that matches investors with viable ventures. These market developments have further built resilience in the domestic market that enables Islamic finance to continuously contribute towards economic developments.
Secondly, the development of strong foundations for Islamic finance has enabled Malaysia to further integrate with the global market.
This is an important milestone in establishing connectivity between financial centres to facilitate greater cross-border Islamic financial transactions. Malaysia is currently the market leader for the sukuk segment with market share of more than 50% in sukuk outstanding since year 2000. Its vibrant marketplace has led to the issuances of multicurrency sukuk in US Dollar, Singapore Dollar, Chinese Renminbi and Japanese Yen as well as attracted foreign issuers to tap the domestic sukuk market including from Singapore, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kazakhstan and China. In terms of financial linkages, Malaysia has also strengthened cooperation with various countries such as the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Turkey, Indonesia and Japan. These bilateral relations have paved the way for stronger Islamic finance’s offerings globally as well as resulted in the appointment of our local players as lead arrangers for some of the global sukuk issuances. These developments also have positive effects to our ancillary service providers where they gained prominence through greater engagement with the international market. It is also interesting that from another perspective, the internationalisation of Islamic finance provides a testimony to the inclusivity and versatility of Islamic finance that has extended beyond religious considerations. Now, customers of Islamic finance has expanded beyond the Muslim community to include customers of diverse backgrounds and origins. Growing presence of Islamic finance can also be observed in non-traditional markets such as in the European countries (e.g. Luxembourg and France), signalling greater acceptance of Islamic finance worldwide. I believe this phenomenon stems from the values and principles embedded in Islamic finance that are universal and cut across boundaries. In this respect, Islamic finance is indeed for all.
The third milestone is Malaysia’s pioneering initiatives and thought leadership in Islamic finance that has enabled Malaysia to advance its innovation in the Islamic finance industry.
Given the commitment to develop Islamic finance into a sustainable financial system, Malaysia has initiatied multiple developments that contributed towards further expansion of Islamic finance both locally and internationally.
Key outcomes are reflected in major developments in the global sukuk market, for example in the issuance of the first sovereign and corporate sukuk. The Malaysian capital market has raised the bar for product innovation in the capital market through various innovative structures. The recent innovation is the issuance of the first Socially Responsible Investment sukuk in 2015 that links returns to the performance of the selected schools which are supported by proceeds from the sukuk investments.
On the regulatory front, our modernisation of the regulatory framework (i.e. IFSA 2013) paves the way for the development of Shariah standards by the Bank. This regulatory initiative presents a monumental step, given its potential to reshape the Islamic financial landscape through enhanced clarity and certainty of Shariah contractual features in both Shariah and operational aspects. We aspire for these standards to be the international benchmark, given their distinct features that include operational guidances to support implementation of Shariah requirements at the institutional level. In our ambition to position these standards as a global reference point, translation work of these standards into Malay and Arabic language, in addition to English, has also been undertaken recently to further expand its outreach.
At the back of such thought leadership lie in-depth research, thorough assessment and knowledge enrichment to provide continuous enhancements in the industry. In this regard, ISRA has played an instrumental role as a dedicated Shariah research arm as well as a knowledge repository for Islamic finance. It is recognised as one of the key players in Islamic finance research globally and has emerged as the top contributor in Islamic finance research between 2011-2013. This is complemented by our effort in capacity building and talent development that allows us to not only produce high-quality human capital but also enable us to export such talent abroad. INCEIF, for example, has enrolled more than 2,000 students from 80 countries and produced over 1,000 graduates to date. With talent enrichment and enhanced thought leadership, Malaysia will ensure continuous innovation in Islamic finance in tandem with the advancements of the market both locally and internationally.
2. What is the, next major milestone for the development of Islamic finance, moving forward?
We have moved from domestic centric to being an international marketplace. Parallel efforts have been taken to develop a comprehensive financial system, while continuing to establish international linkages.
All these initiatives have produced the desired outcomes as envisioned by the Bank. However, the rapid changes and dynamism of the industry require Islamic finance to strive even harder now. True to its name, Islamic finance needs to continuously carve its own branding and distinctiveness to provide wholesome value propositions. On this premise, the next frontier and the major milestone would be positioning Islamic finance to become more prominent and leading agent of positive change for the financial system, and operates within a network economy that is built upon shared values of integrity, inclusivity and sustainability. Greater attention will be devoted to value creation and value-based businesses that reflect the true essence of Islamic finance. What l meant is that Islamic finance moving forward should function as a value-based intermediation by emphasising on value-generating activities that could expand the spectrum of outcomes, which include both monetary gains and social impacts. As you are aware, the global movement towards responsible finance has become more apparent and stronger by the day, and with the increasing inclination towards value-based financial systems in the current atmosphere, Islamic finance is well-positioned to accentuate its innate features and become increasingly relevant in a world that is reorienting towards a greater sense of purpose. Islamic finance stands a great chance to take leadership in this evolution and further activate the market with a new business culture that emanates from its core underlying principles. In my view, there are two enablers that will set Islamic finance in motion in order for it to actualise this higher objective:
Islamic finance to be at the forefront of technology-based finance.
The technological disruption that brings about the advent of fintech opens doors of opportunities for the industry to take Islamic finance to the next level. Technology represents a powerful channel for Islamic finance to further deepen its value propositions and effectively deliver them in a more interconnected information society. Given these prospects, I believe the industry will rise to the occasion through a change in their thinking paradigm. This involves a transformation from a wait-and-see mentality to a more proactive mind-set that aggressively capitalises on technology to innovate and challenge the existing norms. Instead of assuming the role of a mere adherent, the Islamic finance industry should emerge as a leader in technology-based finance that encompasses diverse aspects in financial businesses such as in product development, operational conditions, and even in strategic alliances. The fusion of state-of-the-art features in their future business models will enable the growth of Islamic finance to ride on technology on many fronts to sustain and elevate its positive trajectory. In fact, technological endowments may also advance the current small-scale segments in the industry, in particular enhanced penetration in the takaful sector and greater presence of Islamic finance in financing international trade. The recent establishment of the Investment Account Platform (IAP) as the first banking-intermediated internet-based platform in Islamic finance has already set the momentum for digitisation strategies to be the new normal in the banking business operational model. This development is set as catalyst for further emergence of other innovative delivery channels in Islamic finance that will improve efficiencies, reduce wastage and enhance customers’ overall experiences towards effective delivery of its value offerings.
Islamic finance to inject a culture of innovation into the industry
. The objective to transcend Islamic finance to a leadership position requires reinvention of the existing model that is preconditioned by holistic innovation and modification. At the heart of this requisite is the capacity of our talent to bring in innovative solutions and new approaches to the current system. Efforts to create conducive environment has to be accelerated and accustomed to a culture of innovation that energises talent to introduce new contexts and ideas. From my perspective, one way to encourage the creation of innovative ideas is through stronger industry-academia partnership where outcomes of breakthrough researches could be translated into practical business ideas and industry’s practices. More effective collaboration between these two entities will foster effective information flow between the industries and the universities that ensure consistent understanding in visioning the future of Islamic finance and promoting practical and solution-driven researches. To further invigorate the market environment towards innovation, INCEIF will be organising a symposium to gather both industry players and academicians in a shared platform to develop and test breakthrough ideas in Islamic finance. This medium is envisioned to stimulate continuous generation of inspiring ideas to support innovations in the industry.
B. REGULATION
3. Islamic finance and banking has now been incorporated into the key legislation. We are talking about the Central Banking Act 2009 and the IFSA. Are they sufficient for the moment?
Yes, both the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 (CBA) and IFSA 2013 are sufficient in terms of providing comprehensive legislations for the Islamic finance industry.
The CBA 2009 in particular, has codified the recognition to the Islamic financial system alongside the conventional financial system. It is a very important provision as it reaffirms our commitment to continually develop Islamic finance in a dual financial setting. The Act also elevated the position of the Shariah Advisory Council (SAC) as the highest point of reference in any Islamic financial matters, thus strengthening its authority on Shariah matters as far as banking and takaful is concerned. I believe we are the only Central Bank that has embedded this highest recognition for the SAC in our Act.
The IFSA on the other hand, further modernised the legislative framework for the Islamic finance sector in Malaysia. The Act not only provides for achievement of greater stability and growth of the industry, it also acts as a catalyst for greater legal and operational certainty for stronger end-to-end Shariah compliance. The Act also introduced an important foundation for the evolution of a contract-based regulatory framework for the Islamic financial sector. Furthermore, it has permitted the role of Islamic financial institutions to be expanded to include investment intermediation in addition to its existing credit intermediation. This is expected to further broaden and deepen the avenue for a more diversified Islamic banking business that can attract a wider customer base.
I wish to bring your attention to the distinct provisions under Part IV of the IFSA on Shariah governance requirements. This provision provides greater clarity on the Shariah governance requirements, primarily on the role of the Board and management of the Shariah Committees and in particular the enforcement expectations. An important focus under this provision is the development of Shariah and operational standards for key Shariah contracts which l believe, would foster greater transparency and consistency of Shariah contract applications, thereby leading to greater certainty and strengthened Shariah compliance. Recent amendments to the Development Financial Institutions Act 2002 (DFIA) on Shariah requirements further ensure that the Islamic business activities of our development financial institutions (DFIs) comply with the same Shariah requirements as imposed on Islamic banks under IFSA.
With such legal foundations in place, it is the onus of the industry to capitalise and take full advantage of the opportunities presented by CBA and IFSA in advancing the industry forward. Greater product innovations by Islamic financial institutions are expected to be encouraged through issuance of the various Shariah standards by the Bank. In particular, innovation in the area of investment intermediation would give them the additional competitive edge and at the same time, developing the appropriate expertise and internal system capabilities to identify and monitor the appropriate investment opportunities to support this new line of business.
4. What are the key building blocks still required for Islamic finance on the regulation front?
Before l proceed to answer your question on the key building blocks, let me bring you back to the formation of the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) in 2002, that serves as the global standard setting body to develop prudential standards for Islamic financial institutions. Over the last 14 years, the IFSB has been instrumental in issuing several prudential standards in Islamic banking, takaful and the capital market as part of its efforts to contribute towards the orderly stability of the financial system. In this regards, l wish to share with you an important document issued by the IFSB in 2010 i.e. "The Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability Report" prepared by the Task Force on Islamic Finance and Global Financial Stability headed by the then Governor Zeti. This document encapsulates 8 key building blocks that are fundamental for policymakers worldwide in their efforts to strengthen the resilience and to ensure sustainability of the global Islamic finance industry.
In the Malaysian context, l wish to note that we have implemented all the eight building blocks. For example, in the effective implementation and enforcement of prudential and supervisory standards issued by the IFSB, we have made great strides in this area, in particular by taking these standards into account in the formulation of our policies. Our Shariah Governance Framework for example is derived from the Standards on Islamic Governance Systems. Similarly, our Capital Adequacy Framework for Islamic Banks took several elements of the Capital Adequacy Standard issued by IFSB.
In terms of disclosure requirements, the work undertaken by the Malaysian Accounting Standards Board and Malaysian Institute of Accountants to issue the Financial Reporting Standards for Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) further solidifies our commitment to strengthen the accounting, auditing and disclosure standards of IFIs as to facilitate effective monitoring and assessment of these institutions.
An important building block which is a perennial issue to every IFI in most parts of the world is having in place an effective liquidity management for the industry. The Bank, with several other central banks have established the International Islamic Liquidity Management Corporation (IILM) in 2010, of which Malaysia is a founding member and its host country. The corporation has successfully introduced and facilitated effective cross-border Shariah-compliant liquidity management solutions through the issuance of a series of IILM sukuk issuance to meet the global liquidity demand of the industry. As at 1Q 2016, 23 series of IILM sukuk was issued with a cumulative amount of USD15.38 billion, making the current outstanding amount stand at USD2.2 billion. IILM has also remained as the largest and sole regular short-term sukuk issuer in USD, accounting for 48.9% of global short-term sukuk.
The Bank has also strengthened our financial safety nets for the industry by providing adequate lender of last resort (LOLR) facilities and emergency financing mechanisms, as well as placing a Shariah compliant deposit insurance alongside the conventional deposit insurance.
The Report also highlights the importance of enhancing capacity building and human capital development, in which the Bank shares similar aspirations through our pro-active, holistic and comprehensive approach by setting up the required ecosystem with the establishment of various talent institutions to address talent gaps in the industry.
Other building blocks, such as developing an effective crisis management and resolution framework; as well as the macro-prudential surveillance framework and financial stability analysis which are integral to strengthen the resilience of the industry have been captured in our various policies and guidelines. The rating agencies in Malaysia
[1]
are also actively involved in strengthening the rating processes as to be appreciative of the unique features and risk profiles of Islamic institutions and its instruments.
C. INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT
5. From the central bank perspective, what are the key developments in the industry that has strengthened the industry? Why?
Vision-setting
for Islamic finance industry in the country has enabled coordinated infrastructural developments that solidify domestic market for subsequent international expansion. The BNM’s Financial Sector Masterplan 2001-2010 (FSMP) and The Financial Sector Blueprint 2011-2020 (Blueprint) have outlined strategic reforms and envisioned future Islamic finance landscape to set the motion for the next phase of development in Islamic finance. These comprehensive roadmaps highlight key developments in these three broad areas namely on legislation, institutional building and talent ecosystem. The formulation of these strategic plans sets the overall direction of Islamic finance industry and ensures orderly development of Islamic finance in Malaysia.
In Malaysia, continuous efforts in ensuring an
enabling and accommodative legal infrastructure
are undertaken either through dedicated legislations or amendments to the existing laws. Malaysia’s commitment to institute a dedicated Act for Islamic financial business has begun as early as the enactment of the Islamic Banking Act 1983 (IBA) and the Takaful Act 1984 that paved the way for the establishment of the first Islamic bank and takaful operator. In 2010, the Law Harmonisation Committee (LHC) was then established with a mandate to undertake objective reviews of other relevant laws that may pose legal uncertainty in Islamic finance and recommend appropriate changes to relevant stakeholders in providing legal recognition to Shariah contractual features. This has been important to support the consistency in application of Shariah contracts in Islamic financial transactions. After three decades, the diversity and maturity of the Islamic financial system has led to the development of IFSA 2013 as a significant milestone. It serves as a forward-looking Act that lays down the foundation for future Islamic finance developments as well as strengthens end-to-end Shariah governance and compliance primarily through the Shariah contract-based regulatory framework. As part of the dispute resolution mechanism, regulation on Financial Ombudsman Scheme introduced by the Bank in 2015 is aimed to enhance financial dispute resolution arrangements for consumers and to strengthen consumer protection. The Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration (KLRAC) has also published arbitration rules for Islamic banking and financial services Legal to facilitate legal redress for disputes relating to Islamic financial transactions.
Progressive
institutional building
of Islamic banking players has increased market vibrancy in the Islamic finance industry. From a single player, the Islamic banking sector has grown in numbers following the involvement of conventional players through the Islamic windows set-up. The conducive environment provided by the Bank has facilitated the transformation of these windows into full-fledged Islamic banks licensed under the Islamic Banking Act 1983 and IFSA 2013. At the same time, we also brought forward the liberalisation of the Islamic banking sector by issuing three new licenses to foreign Islamic banks as per our international linkages agenda.
The
establishment of talent ecosystem
comprising talent institutions such as INCEIF, CIIF, IBFIM, ISRA, ICLIF and ASAS enables sustainable development of professional and expertise that is required for Islamic financial services sector in Malaysia. The development of these specialised institutions, aims to develop financial services professional across the various levels, from the entry level for graduate to the leadership level for senior management and board of directors. While we are addressing the talent shortage, we need to orchestrate our effort in producing high-quality talent for Islamic finance covering specific areas like investment, risk management, governance and leadership, IT, capital as well as financial market.
6. What are some of the challenges facing the industry as a whole?
Based on the major milestones that l have deliberated earlier on, Islamic finance industry would be challenged to meet the greater expectations to ensure sustainable growth momentum. Indeed, challenges are inevitable, and l am a strong believer that challenges, and to a certain extent positive disruptions are necessary to stimulate new thinking and approach if we wish to shape Islamic finance to new frontiers. Based on my preliminary observations after taking over the Islamic Banking and Takaful Department, the main issues facing the Islamic finance industry revolve around three broad areas, namely; i) leadership; ii) talent deployment and enrichment; and iii) awareness on Islamic finance.
The latest ‘innovative disruptions’ in the financial sector and the dynamic and fast-paced nature of the current environment leaves no option but for the industry to develop high-calibre talent and leaders in the industry whom are able to measure and assess their business directions, without solely depending on lagging indicators, but infusing leading metrics that align with the latest market trends and developments. Technological advancements through fintech and other solutions are already the megatrend, and the shortfall of effective and visionary leadership that is not able to recognise the vast opportunities in this development and to take actions upon them may prevent the market from making further strides in sustaining its growth. Those who fail to view technology as a stimulus for change may fall into complacency, and the thought that incremental innovation is adequate would find that one day they become irrelevant. As a relatively young industry, Islamic finance should be more nimble in embracing these trends, and hence the greater need of capable leaders with strategic visioning and the ability to implement bold ideas through unconventional ways in executing changes for the industry
Another deeper issue that begs our attention is talent deployment. Despite the proliferation of Islamic finance education and training, we are still grappling with shortage of the right talent to lead and energise innovation and breakthroughs for the industry. Effective talent deployment and enrichment, in my mind, is the way forward in order to ensure existing capabilities are optimised while creating supportive environment that welcomes new ideas and perspectives. This calls for a balanced approach that acknowledges talent and potential strengths across all groups from the senior practitioners to the millennials and deploying them in the most synergistic way. The wealth of experiences among the senior practitioners can be benefitted through coaching and mentoring the young professionals to impart the wisdom and maturity of understanding the intricacies of finance and lessons to be learnt. On the other hand, the millennials whom are exposed to various technological advancements, such as real-time and speedy information gathering and global proliferation of information through social networking, should be seen as the young blood with new frames of mind that can offer fresh outlook and new insights. It is this group of millennials that should be empowered and encouraged to share their thoughts and visions to elevate Islamic finance to be a technology-based and technology driven industry. I believe that with the right talent deployment strategy, the industry will be able to maximise their capacity and unlock the potential strength that already lies within.
On the third challenge, namely low awareness and understanding on Islamic finance, let me share with you some results from a national survey conducted by a leading consulting firm on Islamic finance awareness. We are startled that 53% of customers do not choose Islamic financial products because they are not aware of such products, while 24% of customers opt for conventional products over Islamic financial products as they perceive that there is no difference between these two categories. The survey also finds that 16% of customers still view Islamic financial products as solely for Muslims. These findings glaringly reveal that some misconceptions of Islamic finance still prevail to this day despite the more than three decades of its development in Malaysia. This includes misconceptions on the types of Shariah contracts employed in financial transactions, such as
murabahah
and
bai` `
inah where some quarters view that these contracts carry certain inherent risks, particularly for home financing and in the case of abandoned housing projects. This misconception is indeed untrue as the Shariah Advisory Council has thoroughly deliberated the details of the Shariah contracts used to ensure strong adherence to Shariah requirements. The development of Shariah and operational standards for key Shariah contracts fosters greater certainty and strengthened Shariah compliance, while encouraging a wider range of contracts to be used. The industry also plays a role in providing greater and continuous efforts to raise awareness on Islamic finance, and to address the prevalent misunderstanding on its product in order to promote further appreciation towards the value propositions of Islamic finance. For the takaful segment, raising awareness on takaful offerings is even more crucial in view of the low takaful penetration rate of 14.8% of the total population as compared to 40.5% of that in the insurance sector. Given Malaysia’s protection gap which is estimated to be worth RM2.5 trillion
[2]
, there are immense opportunities for takaful to further penetrate the market. Alongside intensified consumer awareness on takaful, there must also be strengthened market conduct practices of takaful companies to create strong brand reputation that will reinforce the public trust in the ethical product propositions of takaful.
D. SHARIAH ADVISORY COUNCIL (SAC)
7.
How does the council function?
8. What are some of the key contribution of the Council?
As a start, let me give you a brief overview of its background. The Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia (SAC) was established in 1997 and it takes on the role as the ultimate authority for the ascertainment of Islamic law for Islamic financial business.
Since its establishment, the SAC plays a dynamic role in advising the Bank on Shariah issues relating to Islamic financial business carried out by the Bank. It is also a source of reference for Islamic financial institutions, the courts or arbitrators in respect of Islamic finance business. Furthermore, the SAC is also empowered to provide advice to any other persons as may be provided under any written law. These functions, as provided under section 52 of the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 are supported by the autonomy that the SAC has which allows it to determine its own procedures. Their rulings are transparent and supported by written justifications. Over the years, these rulings are hardwired into the Shariah Standards.
It is also important to note that, to reflect the critical role of the SAC, its members are appointed by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong from amongst persons who are qualified in Shariah, or who have knowledge or experience in Shariah, banking, finance, law or other related disciplines.[3]
The SAC, as the final arbiter in the interpretation of Shariah principles on Islamic banking and takaful matters and practices has contributed immensely to the development of the Islamic financial industry in Malaysia. Of particular importance is its role in harmonising and standardising the Shariah rulings relating to Islamic financial business which have led to greater consistency and minimal disputes in the industry.
For the industry, the publication of Shariah Resolutions in Islamic finance that contains the decisions of the SAC has been an important source of reference. This compilation includes the Shariah basis in the underlying issues and the SAC rulings on various contracts, products and other operational matters. The Shariah Resolutions are important documents which have been used extensively by the industry in developing their product offering.
Now, as part of the strategy to strengthen the time-to-market for Shariah pronouncements, the Bank issues press release of SAC statements immediately after the SAC meetings. This release has enabled the industry to be informed of the latest decisions and its impact on their operations.
The most recent and significant initiative relates to the Shariah Standards where the SAC has been instrumental in providing the Shariah pronouncements for 14 Shariah contracts, among others
Murabahah
,
Mudarabah, Musyarakah
,
Tawarruq
, and
Istisna`
. These Standards aim to ensure end-to-end compliance with the Shariah rulings in the structuring of Islamic financial products and services, and is further complemented with the operational requirements to allow realistic implementation of the standards. The Standards also contain optional practices as guidance for the industry, particularly in relation to best practices.
Moving forward, I also envision the SAC to be more dynamically involved in the industry. Firstly, the SAC’s members can leverage the stature by establishing themselves as global thought leaders and Islamic finance spokespersons. This would strengthen their positioning as the focal point of leadership and reference for the industry. Secondly, the SAC has strong potential to influence and shape the Shariah Committees of Islamic financial institutions to consistently be on the ground to ensure that they are able to champion customers’ needs by offering effectual references and solutions accordingly. Thirdly, in the area of research and human capital development, the SAC can also become the medium between the academia and the industry by facilitating the linkage between Shariah research and industry application. This initiative allows the SAC to help the industry in shaping their business models based on the research conducted and to drive innovation. Fourthly, I also believe that the SAC can contribute to the development of new talent in the Islamic financial industry by encouraging the industry to provide and foster more learning avenues and opportunities for Shariah graduates in order to generate qualified individuals whom are better able to contribute towards the development of the industry.
9. Reference to the SAC for court cases has been mandatory? How does this work?
In regards to this question, I must make it clear that as stated under Section 56 of the CBA 2009, when Shariah issues are raised in court proceedings, reference to the SAC can be made by the court. To facilitate this process, the Bank has issued the “Manual for Reference by the Court and Arbitrators to the Shariah Advisory Council of Bank Negara Malaysia” that provides guidance on what constitute Shariah matters; the expected time frame to respond; and the rights to be heard by the parties which could be in writing and/or orally.
Essentially, it is also important to know that there are a few procedures and processes that need to be carried out prior to making reference to the SAC by the court. Firstly, before submitting a reference regarding Shariah issues to the SAC, the court and the arbitrator should refer to the published SAC decisions. If the court or arbitrator wishes to obtain more clarity on the Shariah issues, they may contact the SAC Secretariat to obtain information regarding the decisions. In the event that the issue is not available in the published documents or after clarifying with the SAC Secretariat, the court or arbitrator may refer the issue to the SAC.
The manual has explicitly provided the types of Shariah issues that can be referred to the SAC and it must relate to matters that have been or have not been decided by the SAC. These questions include and are not limited to aspects of Islamic financial business such as business structures, products or services, implementations or operations, terms and conditions or documentation.
I wish to clarify that in responding to Shariah issues posed by the court or the arbitrator, the SAC’s role is only to ascertain matters relating to the Islamic law. The SAC does not have the jurisdiction to make findings of fact, to apply law or to make a decision on an issue or case. It is because only the court or the arbitrator has the jurisdiction to do so.
Once the SAC receives the issues from the court or the arbitrator, the SAC will identify and analyse the Shariah issues to ascertain the relevant applicable Islamic law. The court or the arbitrator will then make the decision by applying the Islamic law ascertained by the SAC on the case. After the SAC has made the decision on the Shariah issues raised by the court and arbitrators, it is mandatory on the court and arbitrators to be guided by the decision made.
10.
Some quarters have suggested that it was unprecedented that another body outside of the courts - i.e. the SAC - makes a decision that is binding on the courts. Some have questioned the constitutionality of such SAC decisions? What is the current thinking on this matter at the central bank?
I believe that it is very important for the public to comprehend that the role of SAC is limited and confined exclusively to the ascertainment of the Islamic law on Islamic financial business. Even though Section 57 of the CBA 2009 states that the court is bound by the ruling of the SAC, it does not detract the court from its judicial functions to resolve the disputes brought and submitted by the parties. This statement can be further supported by the Tan Sri Khalid Ibrahim vs. Bank Islam court case which highlights the importance of the SAC in resolving Islamic banking disputes without usurping the judicial power of the court.
I would like to again emphasise that both civil and Islamic laws are required in resolving any Islamic banking disputes raised by the parties. However, given the defined role of the SAC, it is not legally empowered to perform any judicial function in determining the ultimate outcome of litigation. The judicial function to decide on the issues pleaded by parties remains with the court with the SAC as a reference point because the courts are well equipped only to adjudicate civil law issues whereas they are not trained to determine issues of Shariah compliance or non-compliance. As emphasised by Tun Hamid the former Chief Justice, the SAC would only state the principle as required by Shariah instead of saying whether the agreement is valid or otherwise. It is the court that will make a finding of facts and will apply the principles to the facts in order to arrive at a decision. Hence, the SAC’s involvement will in turn ensure a speedy and efficient ruling on an issue.
___________________________________________
[1] Malaysian Rating Corporation Berhad (MARC) provides ratings on a wide range of Shariah-compliant issuances by both domestic and foreign companies in the Ringgit-denominated Sukuk market. MARC’s “Islamic Financial Institution Governance Ratings” introduced in 2010 provides a structured assessment of the quality of institutional governance in an IFI. MARC is also a technical partner to Islamic Development Bank (IDB)-initiated Bahrain-based Islamic International Rating Agency as part of efforts to create a sustainable and dedicated Islamic credit rating institution. RAM Rating Services Berhad (RAM) also provides ratings on a number of Islamic securities.
[2] Based on a comparative study by the Malaysian Takaful Association and Actuarial Partners
[3] The New Shariah Governance Framework 2009

Governor's Remarks at the 5th PETRONAS Board Audit Committee (BAC) Forum - “Audit as a Partner of Change”
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Lanai Kijang
Delivery Date
:
16 Aug. 2016
The theme of today’s forum “
Audit as a Partner of Change”
is highly relevant and timely, as the events in the global market today, involving failures of large firms, frauds and market manipulation activities, underscores the criticality of the three lines of defenses in organizations. For confidence and trust to be restored in the marketplace, the role of the BAC and internal auditors as the third line of defense will be even more critical than ever.
Our role as members of audit committees is much broader than what we may perceive it to be. Organisations such as PETRONAS are widely regarded as amongst the few key flag bearers for the country. Hence, it is incumbent upon the Board and the BAC members to be strong and energetic in upholding the highest standards of professionalism, ethics and integrity in discharging their roles and responsibilities. The people of Malaysia must have confidence and pride that an institution entrusted with much strategic natural resources are run with utmost integrity and professionalism.
Before I proceed further on the topic for today, allow me to touch briefly on the current outlook on the global and domestic economy. The global economy has experienced multiple shocks in recent years, with its effects reverberating across the globe. Global growth has continuously underperformed expectations and is expected to remain moderate going forward.
The divergence in monetary policy in advanced and emerging economies as well as the unexpected policy adjustments in several economies have also culminated in a global environment of heightened volatility and uncertainties. One of the most significant developments we have experienced thus far is the sharp volatility in commodity prices which has created destabilising implications on commodity-driven countries. Amid a confluence of shocks, ranging from weaker-than-expected growth prospects to geopolitical uncertainty and moderation in China’s economic growth, oil prices declined by more than 50% in a span of 6 months in 2014. The volatility in oil prices has also been heightened by unanticipated economic and geo-political developments. The events unfolding in the United Kingdom and consequent effect to the European region have also contributed to the increased volatility in oil prices. Oil prices rallied to above USD50 per barrel from an average of USD33 per barrel in the first quarter of the year, and today, oil prices have settled back to around USD48 per barrel.
The oil price is likely to remain volatile over the next few years due to oversupply and record-high oil inventories against slow demand especially in China. LNG prices are also expected to remain low for a protracted period of time. LNG capacity start-ups in Australia and North America which will boost new LNG supplies amidst stagnating demand will put more pressure on LNG prices, hence further disrupting the LNG market. Due to low oil and LNG prices, the profitability of oil majors and National Oil Companies (NOCs) has been severely eroded. The impact has been pronounced. More than 300,000 oil and gas workers have been laid off globally since mid-2014; some USD 380 billion of global oil and gas projects have been deferred or cancelled; and more than USD 150 billion worth of assets have been planned for disposal or divestment.
Given Malaysia’s openness and high financial and trade integration with the rest of the world, the Malaysian economy is not isolated from these developments. On the external front, lower global demand continues to weigh down on Malaysia’s export performance.
Investment activities especially in the upstream oil and gas sector, contracted for the first time since the global financial crisis in 2015, after expanding by an average of 16% from 2010 to 2014. However, investment activity in the manufacturing and services sectors remained resilient, and is expected to underpin investment growth moving forward. Private consumption remained relatively resilient and anchored domestic growth, especially during the first half of the year, driven by sustained income and employment levels. Going forward, domestic demand is expected to remain a key driver of economic growth in Malaysia. We should expect Malaysian economic growth to range between 4.0 to 4.5 % for 2016.
Amid the changes in the financial landscape, there have been equally significant developments in the auditing standards both globally and locally. The standards and regulations are becoming increasingly tighter and more stringent. The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) for example, has proposed several changes to the Internal Audit Standards, which are expected to take effect in January 2017. The changes to the Standards are aimed at reinforcing the fundamental principles of internal auditing practices, promoting a broad range of value-added internal auditing and fostering improved organisational processes and operations. The direction of changes in the financial reporting standards also places more accountability on the Audit Committees to provide strong oversight on the organisation’s financial reporting and internal controls. The new Companies Bill 2015 (the Bill) was passed by the Dewan Rakyat and is anticipated to come into force by end-2016. The new law is expected to bring major reforms to our corporate landscape and will place greater pressures on the audit function to understand the emerging regulatory requirements and their impact on business operations.
In the wake of uncertainties due to the global developments, the change in regulatory standards and technological advancement require businesses and regulators to think beyond conventional norms in order to navigate through these unchartered waters.
Turning to the theme today, the importance of an independent and effective internal audit function as a core line of defense with a strong Audit Committee in business cannot be overemphasized.
The fundamentals of an internal audit function involve identifying risks that could threaten the viability of the company and keep it from achieving its goals, ensuring management fully understands these risks, and proactively recommending improvements to minimise these risks. Internal auditors are essentially the eyes and ears of the Audit Committee and the overall Board. The failure of audit functions can result in devastating consequences as seen in recent times.
The case of the British Petroleum (BP) oil rig explosion in 2010 is one that reinforces the important role of the internal audit function. Occupational safety is widely regarded as a critical success factor for a company that undertakes oil exploration. The BP oil rig was awarded as the industry model for safety in 2009. However, in 2010, the oil rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, causing one of the worst man-made disasters in history. The U.S investigation commission attributed the disaster to the “failure of individuals involved to identify risks they faced and to properly evaluate, communicate and address them”. This indirectly highlighted the shortcomings of the internal audit function as a contributory source of failure in the lines of defence in the company. Some level of scepticism to consider the remote possibility that the safety measures in place may not work in the event of disaster, could have avoided the risk event from occurring.
Another example is the LIBOR manipulation scandal involving several banks which culminated in substantial fines imposed by the UK Financial Services Authority (FSA). In its internal audit report published in March 2013, the FSA highlighted several issues pertaining to the breakdown of the internal audit function, which led to the manipulation of the rates. Despite the Group internal audit functions carrying out their routine audits in this area, deficiencies in the banks’ systems, controls and policies were not adequately highlighted.
The lessons learnt from the above cases and others clearly reinforce the key roles played by both the internal audit function and the Audit Committee. My view is that the strength and effectiveness of the internal audit function will influence the risk and compliance culture in an organisation. The function has to continually be refreshed such that it remains robust and effective.
Clearly, the job is now more difficult and challenging than ever, given the increased expectations by stakeholders and heightened scrutiny when things go wrong, as well as increasing obligations under the statute that place additional fiduciary responsibilities on audit committee members. I would like to share my thoughts on four matters where efforts are necessary to raise the bar on audit standards and audit quality.
Firstly, the audit coverage and scope should not be confined to compliance or risk-based parameters. The audit scope should be holistic, encompassing new risk areas and tail risk events that originate from the evolving operating environment and financial landscape. The process of ascertaining the audit scope must be robust, such that audits focus on higher risk areas as the company grows and evolves in its products and processes. Internal auditors should be constantly challenged to think beyond the scope of the audit framework and focus on the broader picture. The so-called ability to ‘connect the dots’ about the implications of the audit findings across the organisation is an important starting point to identify new and emerging risks.
Secondly, internal audit should move beyond compliance to strategic auditing and to provide value-added recommendations for the betterment of the organisation. My view is that before an organisation seeks to venture into new or higher risk areas of growth, it is imperative for the board and senior management to seek assurance from the internal audit function so that the risk and control frameworks are rigorous in identifying gaps in the system. The Audit Committee should identify opportunities where the internal audit function is able to add value, through consultation and advice on business process improvements. The input from the internal audit function would also be helpful to craft initiatives to embed good behavioural norms, ethical and responsible culture within the organisation.
Thirdly, the internal audit function must be supported by a strong quality assurance process. This requires internal auditors to be equipped with the requisite skills such that they are able to leverage on their expertise and experience to make sound judgement and challenge the norm. This becomes even more important as companies grow in scale, venture into new lines of business and become more complex. Further, the internal audit function should leverage on technology as a key enabler to improve audit quality and audit effectiveness. Innovation in audit techniques should be promoted with greater usage of data analytic tools for better risk profiling and sampling.
There ought to be close engagement between the internal audit function and external auditors on key risks and systemic issues, and in strengthening the overall assurance process.
Fourth, the role of the Audit Committee is integral in these efforts. The Audit Committee at the apex needs to exercise strong oversight through setting the “tone from the top” and embedding the right culture to ensure that the internal audit function is independent and objective in delivering its mandates. One message of ‘tone from the top’ is a reminder to all Heads of Internal Audit that any findings that might indicate unethical or fraudulent activities or have reputational impact to PETRONAS should be communicated to the BAC immediately without waiting for the BAC to meet. There should be ‘zero tolerance’ for any cases that involve abuses and corrupt practices.
Another important imperative is the Committee’s responsibility to design governance structures that avoid placing the internal audit function in conflicted positions, and ensure that the function has sufficient standing and authority within the organisation. This will help to strengthen the ability of the internal audit function to independently audit and raise red flags where risks are observed. Direct accessibility to the Audit Committee is key in this respect.
Concluding remarks
As the world becomes more interconnected, an effective organisation will see its business managers and control functions partnering with the auditors, leveraging on their skills to build more effective operations, and strengthen business prospects. Audit as a partner of change lies on the ability of the organisation to adapt and collaborate with the auditors towards securing the organisation’s long term success.

Governor's Speech at the Launch of the Educator’s Manual on Shariah Standard Murabahah
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Multipurpose Hall, Lanai Kijang
Delivery Date
:
15 Aug. 2016
We are here today to witness the launch of the Educator’s Manual on Shariah Standard Murabahah. The Manual is a pioneering effort. Translating the Shariah standard and operational requirements into a user-friendly format for adoption in the academic syllabus of our local universities will go a long way in enhancing the Islamic finance syllabus by educational establishment.
This is a great team effort. I would like to congratulate the panel of authors that have tirelessly contributed towards the production of this teaching guide. The Shariah Advisory Council (SAC) members, researchers from the International Shari’ah Research Academy (ISRA), representatives from the Islamic Banking and Finance Institute Malaysia (IBFIM), the academic fraternity and the industry players. The dedication of the team has produced a manual that will make the overall learning experience more comprehensive, exciting and interactive.
My congratulations and appreciation to Universiti Sains Islam Malaysia (USIM) and the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) for being visionary to participate in this pilot project. There is a wealth of benefits to be gained. It is our aspiration that other universities would be a part of this initiative that would contribute towards enhancing the quality of our Islamic finance education.
For the past three decades, Islamic finance in Malaysia has undergone a journey that is marked with various significant milestones. I would like to highlight three major achievements of the industry in term of its development since inception. Firstly, Islamic finance in the country has become a key segment in the financial system. What was once a novelty is now mainstream. This is a consequence of continuous initiatives to build a solid foundation, focusing on infrastructural, institutional and capacity building measures, as well as robust regulatory and supervisory framework. These measures are the cornerstones of Islamic finance industry’s growth.
From less than four Islamic banks and takaful players before year 2000, there are now 27 players that offer over 100 financial products beyond the basic financial offerings. The industry is characterised by increasing competitiveness and innovation. The recently launched Investment Account Platform (IAP) is the latest initiative where the industry has cooperated to further enhance the offerings of Islamic banks. The IAP provides an online marketplace to match potential investors with viable ventures. Islamic banking assets have also grown beyond the targeted 20% as originally intended in Bank Negara Malaysia’s Financial Sector Masterplan.
It now stands at more than a quarter (27%) of the total banking system. Islamic finance also provides financing to all segments of society irrespective of beliefs, race and gender. There is also greater acceptance of takaful with its increased penetration rate to 14.8% of the population. For over 3 decades, Islamic finance has grown and developed and contributed significantly to the development of the real economy.
Secondly, enhanced integration with the global market has enabled greater trade and financial linkages. Malaysia is now positioned at the forefront of international developments with increasing connectivity between financial centres, and more cross-border Islamic financial transactions. Our sukuk market constitutes more than 50% of global sukuk outstanding for the past 16 years. Malaysia as an international Islamic finance marketplace offers an attractive and facilitative platform for foreign issuers to tap our domestic sukuk market. There have been various issuances of multicurrency sukuk in US Dollar, Singapore Dollar, Chinese Renminbi and Japanese Yen. There are also stronger bilateral ties with various countries such as the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Turkey, Indonesia and Japan.
These interlinkages open up greater opportunities to introduce and strategically position Islamic finance services globally while providing opportunities for meaningful participation of our local players as lead arrangers for some of the global sukuk issuances. The gains are also extended to our ancillary service providers that were able to establish greater connections with the international market.
Thirdly, Malaysia’s pioneering initiatives and thought leadership in Islamic finance has enabled the country to advance innovation in the Islamic finance industry. On the regulatory front, the modernisation of the regulatory framework through the Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 (IFSA) provides an opportunity and space for Islamic financial institutions to offer new products and services.
The launch that we are witnessing today is a major initiative, the development of a Shariah standard that is integrated with details on operational requirements. This approach ensures a transparent basis of Shariah rulings by the SAC, and provides a convergent in understanding between Shariah scholars and industry practitioners. In judiciary matters, where the SAC serves as a reference point in analysing muamalat cases, the court can also draw on these comprehensive and transparent Shariah standards as basis in arriving at a court ruling. The adoption of the standards by learning institutions will pave the way for greater understanding and acceptance of these standards as a global starting point of reference for the Islamic finance community.
As we launch the Educator’s Manual, which is the first of 14 series of manuals, I would like to share my thoughts on our approach in developing the Shariah standards, and would also like to emphasise the importance of embracing diversity and mutual respect in Shariah interpretations. I shall deliberate on two additional areas that stakeholders need to consider to maximise the benefits of having the Manual; reconfiguration of academic programmes and strategising talent deployment.
The future growth of Islamic finance, especially cross border, is very much dependent on the harmonisation and mutual recognition of Shariah views and rulings across the globe. It is critical if cross border trades are to be strengthened. Numerous efforts are being pursued to narrow the opinion gaps between scholars through symposiums, roundtables as well as bilateral dialogues. However, narrowing of Shariah opinions is preferable but not critical. The fact is, differences in views and opinions among scholars are a historical fact, and an accepted facet in the area of Shariah, particularly in matters relating to fiqh muamalat (jurisprudence). In fact, my own view is that great Islamic civilisation of yesteryears was possible and the envy of many because of our diversity, tolerance and mutual respect of each other’s view.
In the context of the Shariah Standards, the dynamic process of its development involves the act of harmonising the differences and embracing diversity. We respect views of others which are different from ours by looking into the wisdom of earlier scholars from all recognised schools of thought (Mazhabs). We are also willing to arrive at new rulings where it is appropriate. This broadens the reference scope for Shariah scholars to have an enriching debate on the best application of Shariah in contemporary finance, based on the customs, legal and operational framework of each market. This is an important principle, as it increases the depth of fiqh research that leads to greater understanding of practices in Muamalat through the times while recognising the influence of local tradition, as well as domestic business practices. The act of balancing the authenticity and practicality of the different Shariah interpretations is an important component in seeking a solution for the benefits and welfare of the ummah.
In this respect, the guiding philosophy of the SAC has always been to formulate a collective ijtihad or Shariah rulings that are comprehensive, inclusive and pragmatic, without sacrificing the sacred objectives of Shariah.
I very much believe in the importance of embracing diversity in Shariah interpretations within the academic community. Students who are exposed to the teachings of all schools of thought from the very beginning would get to appreciate the intellectual differences and value the flexibility arising from differing opinions. This provides an opportunity to open and sharpen their minds and widen their thinking by exploring issues from multidimensional perspectives. Through this way, the talent that we nurture and produce would not only be equipped with Shariah know-hows, but also with intellectual courage that can articulate contemporary Shariah issues in the context of domestic customs and business environment.
I would like to expand my thoughts on the two additional areas that, if pursued could further enhance stakeholder gains from the Educator’s Manual:
First, is the reconfiguration of academic programmes to nurture talent with enhanced employability; and
Second, strategising talent deployment to reduce time to competency.
Reconfiguration of academic programmes
Continuous enhancements of curriculums in universities are critical to increase the employability factor of our students. These include reconfiguration of the academic programmes at universities and enhancements to the learning tools and methods of teaching. This adds to the traditional pedagogy to ensure its dynamism through evolving times, while providing the right learning environment that can challenge the minds and sharpen the skills and experience of our students. One such addition is experiential learning.
The adoption of experiential learning opens the window of opportunity for students to go beyond theory-based teaching. Examples include industry-wide internship, real life problem solving assignments and apprenticeship programmes for students. These methods create greater connection between classroom learning with the real world. I believe this form of experiential learning is a strong stimulant to knowledge acquisition that encourages students to develop their skills while experiencing responsible decision making in real-time. Experience in real life situations differentiates experiential learning from cognitive and behavioural learning. This provides the students with a competitive edge and increases the probability of success for graduates at entry-level into the workforce.
Islamic finance industry can contribute significantly towards experiential learning. Malaysia, with its long history that includes the development of Islamic finance over three decades is content rich and ideal for case study research. There are many matters and areas that require in-depth research and solutions. The case study method is another popular learning tool that has proven to be effective in enhancing and strengthening critical appraisal and understanding among students. The case study method also provides an opportunity to discuss multiple perspectives in dealing with issues.
Within the Islamic finance realm, prospective cases studies can include amongst others the application of Shariah Standards by Islamic banks and its effects on product structuring and pricing strategy, legal aspects, risk management, oversight function and governance process of the banks. For the takaful sector, case studies on microtakaful for example can lead to the development of protection schemes that can be offered at affordable prices. I trust the academia has enough resources to produce such case studies and generate new research findings and breakthroughs, given the knowledge and expertise of their academic faculties.
In essence, we need to be more exploratory and brave to rigorously investigate or examine real life situations and complex scenarios and benefit from hindsight and learnt lessons that can give new solutions for future growth.
The initiative to develop the Educator’s Manual is in itself a good starting point to encourage universities to move towards experiential learning. Students will be exposed to Shariah and operational requirements covering areas such as product structuring, legal, accounting as well as risk management. The transparent nature of the standards would enable students to critique and form their own views and conclusions. It is a leap forward to change the paradigm on the theoretical and operational aspects of Shariah applications. This initiative is certainly a game-changer for our Islamic finance education programme.
This initiative is also an important milestone in terms of academia-industry cooperation in equipping our students with industry relevant and contemporary application of Shariah contracts in Islamic financial products and services.
Given the new content on the subject matter, a pre-condition to successfully implement the learning guide is to train and expose lecturers to multiple disciplines of subject matters. Particularly, as the applications of the Shariah and operational requirements cover various fields that include legal, accounting, risk management and information technology. Developmental training is a critical component as it enables the imparting of knowledge effectively.
Strategising talent deployment
While it is acknowledged that the role of learning institutions is essential to develop talent with higher skill sets, the industry also has an important role to ensure effective deployment of graduates as they enter the workforce. The number of graduates is indeed increasing at a rapid rate. The general feedback of Shariah graduates however is the lack of opportunities for employment. But the reality is that the industry still grapples with shortage of the right talent that can lead and energise innovation. A solution is to reconcile the expectation gaps of the industry and graduates. Talent enrichment program is one area where we can pursue to bring out the best of student talent. Enrichment programmes in areas beyond Shariah, such as leadership training at the early stage of recruitment would strengthen the confidence of Shariah students and provide the required exposure for them to understand and appreciate the intricacies of business environment.
Over the years, the Bank established specialised institutions to enrich the talent ecosystem. These institutions, namely INCEIF, ISRA, IBFIM, the Chartered Institute of Islamic Finance Professionals (CIIF) and the Association of Shariah Advisors in Islamic Finance Malaysia (ASAS) have collectively contributed towards sustainable development of professionals and expertise in the industry.
I am pleased to note that the industry has significantly benefitted from the contribution of these institutions. INCEIF is now widely recognised as a global university in Islamic finance and has enrolled more than 2,000 students from 80 countries and produced over 1,000 graduates to date. ISRA plays an instrumental role as a dedicated Shariah research arm as well as a knowledge repository for Islamic finance. It is known as one of the key players in Islamic finance research globally and has emerged as the top contributor in Islamic finance research between 2011-2013. IBFIM, which is the industry training arm, has also made significant achievements with over 6,400 participants attending its training programmes in 2015. In raising the bar of professionalism, the Chartered Institute of Islamic Finance Professionals as the first professional body in Islamic finance seeks to promote the highest standards of professional practice amongst Islamic finance practitioners. Two standards on the admission of members and accreditation of institutions have been issued in November last year and two more are anticipated in 2016. ASAS, with prominent scholars as its members, has also embarked on various initiatives that have contributed towards its objective of inculcating the highest level of professionalism of Shariah advisors.
Despite all these achievements, we must admit that there is no room for complacency. We must continue to establish new grounds and set new thresholds for our organisations towards greater success. In this context, I am pleased to inform that the Bank will be forming a Steering Committee made up of representatives from both industry and academia to undertake an in-depth review of the strategic positioning of these important organisations. It is as part of our efforts to re-energise and reinvent the Islamic finance talent development landscape.
Conclusion
The collective efforts of everyone here today will determine the path of Islamic finance moving forward. A simple yet meaningful event to witness the launching of the Educator’s Manual today will be an important learning tool for many of our future students. I wish to record again our sincere thanks for the contribution and commitment of many people, particularly from the panel of authors and members of academia and wish everyone continuous success for the upcoming series of the future manuals.
Dengan lafaz Bismillahirrahmanirrahim, saya melancarkan Educator’s Manual on Shariah Standard Murabahah.
Thank you.
